solution:
The mean square speed of the molecules of a gas is fixed by the absolute temperature alone:

\( \dfrac{1}{2} m \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} = \dfrac{3}{2} k_{B} T \quad \Rightarrow \quad \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} = \dfrac{3 k_{B} T}{m} \), so \( \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} \propto T \) for a given gas.

Both temperatures are already in kelvin, so no conversion is needed.

\( \dfrac{\overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}}_{1}}{\overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}}_{2}} = \dfrac{T_{1}}{T_{2}} = \dfrac{30 \text{ K}}{120 \text{ K}} = \dfrac{1}{4} \)

**Ratio of mean square speeds \( = 1 : 4 \).**

Note that the question asks for the MEAN SQUARE speeds, which go as \( T \). Had it asked for the root mean square speeds the answer would have been \( \sqrt{1/4} = 1 : 2 \).

Write the ideal gas equation in the form that contains the NUMBER OF MOLECULES:

\( PV = N k_{B} T \quad \Rightarrow \quad N = \dfrac{PV}{k_{B} T} \)

Let vessel B have pressure \( P \), volume \( V \) and temperature \( T \). Then vessel A has \( 2P \), \( 2V \) and \( 2T \).

For vessel B: \( N_{B} = \dfrac{P V}{k_{B} T} \)

For vessel A: \( N_{A} = \dfrac{(2P)(2V)}{k_{B} (2T)} = \dfrac{4 P V}{2 k_{B} T} = \dfrac{2 P V}{k_{B} T} \)

\( \therefore \dfrac{N_{A}}{N_{B}} = \dfrac{2 P V / k_{B} T}{P V / k_{B} T} = 2 \)

**\( N_{A} : N_{B} = 2 : 1 \).**

The temperature doubling cancels half of the fourfold increase produced by doubling both \( P \) and \( V \); vessel A holds twice as many molecules, not four times. (\( k_{B} \) cancels, so no numerical value of it is needed, and it does not matter that the gas is the same in both vessels beyond ensuring that "number of molecules" means the same thing in each.)

The kinetic-theory expression for the pressure of a gas is

\( P = \dfrac{1}{3} \dfrac{N}{V} m \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} \)

where \( m \) is the mass of one molecule and \( \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} \) the mean square speed. The number of molecules \( N \) and the volume \( V \) of the cylinder are unchanged.

New mass: \( m' = \dfrac{m}{3} \)

New speed: \( \mathrm{v}' = 2\mathrm{v} \), so the MEAN SQUARE speed becomes \( \overline{\mathrm{v}'^{2}} = (2)^{2}\, \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} = 4\, \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} \) — the speed is squared in the pressure formula, so doubling it multiplies that factor by 4, not by 2.

\( P' = \dfrac{1}{3} \dfrac{N}{V} \left( \dfrac{m}{3} \right) \left( 4 \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} \right) = \dfrac{4}{3} \left[ \dfrac{1}{3} \dfrac{N}{V} m \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} \right] = \dfrac{4}{3} P \)

**Resultant pressure \( = \dfrac{4}{3} P \approx 1.33 P \)** — the pressure INCREASES, to four-thirds of its original value.

The rms speed of the molecules of a gas of molar mass \( M_{0} \) at absolute temperature \( T \) is

\( \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{rms}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3 R T}{M_{0}}} \)

Both gases are at S.T.P., so \( T \) is the SAME (273 K) for both, and \( R \) is a universal constant. Hence at a common temperature

\( \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{rms}} \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{M_{0}}} \)

Molar masses: for oxygen \( \mathrm{O}_{2} \), \( M_{0} = 2 \times 16 = 32 \) g \( \text{mol}^{-1} \); for sulfur dioxide \( \mathrm{SO}_{2} \), \( M_{0} = 32 + 2 \times 16 = 64 \) g \( \text{mol}^{-1} \).

\( \dfrac{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{rms}} (\mathrm{O}_{2})}{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{rms}} (\mathrm{SO}_{2})} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT / M_{\mathrm{O}_{2}}}{3RT / M_{\mathrm{SO}_{2}}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{M_{\mathrm{SO}_{2}}}{M_{\mathrm{O}_{2}}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{64}{32}} = \sqrt{2} \)

\( \therefore \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{rms}} (\mathrm{O}_{2}) = \sqrt{2}\ \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{rms}} (\mathrm{SO}_{2}) \), which is what was to be shown.

Note the ratio is INVERTED relative to the masses: the lighter molecule (\( \mathrm{O}_{2} \), 32) is the faster one, and the heavier \( \mathrm{SO}_{2} \) is slower by the factor \( \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414 \). Because both gases are at the same temperature, their molecules have the same average kinetic energy, so the heavier ones must move more slowly.

\( \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{rms}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3 R T}{M_{0}}} \)

At S.T.P. the helium is at \( T_{\mathrm{He}} = 273 \text{ K} \). Let \( T \) be the required temperature of the oxygen. Molar masses: \( M_{\mathrm{O}_{2}} = 32 \), \( M_{\mathrm{He}} = 4 \).

The two rms speeds are to be equal:

\( \sqrt{\dfrac{3 R T}{32}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3 R \times 273}{4}} \)

Squaring and cancelling \( 3R \):

\( \dfrac{T}{32} = \dfrac{273}{4} \)

\( T = \dfrac{32 \times 273}{4} = 8 \times 273 = 2184 \text{ K} \)

**Required temperature \( = 2184 \text{ K} \)** (that is, \( 2184 - 273 = 1911\ ^\circ \text{C} \)).

The result is a temperature, so it must be quoted in kelvin. It is eight times 273 K because oxygen is eight times as heavy as helium, and \( \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{rms}}^{2} \propto T / M_{0} \) — the oxygen has to be eight times hotter, on the ABSOLUTE scale, to make up for being eight times heavier.

\( \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{rms}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3 R T}{M_{0}}} \), so \( \dfrac{\mathrm{v}_{1}}{\mathrm{v}_{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{T_{1} / M_{1}}{T_{2} / M_{2}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{T_{1}}{T_{2}} \times \dfrac{M_{2}}{M_{1}}} \)

Convert BOTH temperatures to kelvin first — this is the step the question is really testing:

hydrogen: \( T_{1} = 127\ ^\circ \text{C} = 127 + 273 = 400 \text{ K} \), \( M_{1} = 2 \)

oxygen: \( T_{2} = 27\ ^\circ \text{C} = 27 + 273 = 300 \text{ K} \), \( M_{2} = 32 \)

\( \dfrac{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{H}_{2}}}{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{O}_{2}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{400}{300} \times \dfrac{32}{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{4}{3} \times 16} = \sqrt{\dfrac{64}{3}} = \dfrac{8}{\sqrt{3}} \)

Numerically \( \dfrac{8}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{8}{1.732} = 4.619 \).

**\( \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{rms}} (\mathrm{H}_{2}) : \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{rms}} (\mathrm{O}_{2}) = 8 : \sqrt{3} \approx 4.62 : 1 \)** — the hydrogen molecules are about 4.6 times faster.

Had the Celsius values been used directly the ratio would have come out as \( \sqrt{(127/27) \times 16} = 8.68 \), which is wrong; the rms-speed formula holds only for absolute temperature.

From the kinetic theory, \( PV = \dfrac{1}{3} N m \overline{\mathrm{v}^{2}} = \dfrac{2}{3} E \), where \( E \) is the total translational kinetic energy of the gas. Hence

\( E = \dfrac{3}{2} P V \)

Convert the volume to SI units. \( 1 \text{ cc} = 1 \text{ cm}^{3} = 10^{-6} \text{ m}^{3} \), so

\( V = 5000 \text{ cc} = 5000 \times 10^{-6} = 5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}^{3} \)

Standard pressure \( P = 1.013 \times 10^{5} \text{ N/m}^{2} \).

\( E = \dfrac{3}{2} \times \left( 1.013 \times 10^{5} \right) \times \left( 5 \times 10^{-3} \right) \)

\( = 1.5 \times 506.5 = 759.75 \text{ J} \)

**Kinetic energy \( = 759.75 \text{ J} \approx 7.598 \times 10^{2} \text{ J} \).**

No temperature is needed: the pressure and volume between them already fix the total kinetic energy, since \( E = \tfrac{3}{2} PV \). (This is the TRANSLATIONAL kinetic energy, which for a monatomic gas is the whole of the internal energy.)

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives \( 1.558 \times 10^{2} \) J for part (ii), the energy per kilogram. That is smaller than the correct value by a factor of exactly \( 10^{3} \), and it is refuted by the key's OWN part (i): a kilomole of oxygen is 32 kg, so part (ii) must be part (i) divided by 32, namely \( 4.986 \times 10^{6} / 32 = 1.558 \times 10^{5} \) J \( \text{kg}^{-1} \). The printed numeral 155.8 is the energy per GRAM (\( 4986 / 32 \)), so the exponent belongs to joule per gram, not joule per kilogram. A sanity check settles it independently: a single mole of oxygen, only 32 g, already carries 4986 J at this temperature, so one kilogram cannot carry 156 J. The correct answer is \( 1.558 \times 10^{5} \) J \( \text{kg}^{-1} \); parts (i) and (iii) of the printed key are correct.]

Oxygen at \( 127\ ^\circ \text{C} \), i.e. \( T = 127 + 273 = 400 \text{ K} \). Given \( R = 8.31 \) J \( \text{mol}^{-1} \text{K}^{-1} \), \( N_{A} = 6.02 \times 10^{23} \) molecules \( \text{mol}^{-1} \), and molecular weight of oxygen 32.

The average translational kinetic energy of one MOLE is

\( E_{\text{mol}} = \dfrac{3}{2} R T = 1.5 \times 8.31 \times 400 = 4986 \text{ J mol}^{-1} \)

**(i) Per kilomole.** \( 1 \text{ kmol} = 10^{3} \text{ mol} \):

\( E = 4986 \times 10^{3} = 4.986 \times 10^{6} \text{ J kmol}^{-1} \)

**(ii) Per kilogram.** A kilomole of oxygen has a mass of 32 kg (a mole has a mass of 32 g). Dividing the per-kilomole figure by that mass:

\( E = \dfrac{4.986 \times 10^{6} \text{ J}}{32 \text{ kg}} = 1.558 \times 10^{5} \text{ J kg}^{-1} \)

Equivalently, directly: \( \dfrac{3}{2} \dfrac{R}{M_{0}} T = 1.5 \times \dfrac{8.31}{0.032} \times 400 = 1.558 \times 10^{5} \text{ J kg}^{-1} \).

**(iii) Per molecule.** \( k_{B} = \dfrac{R}{N_{A}} = \dfrac{8.31}{6.02 \times 10^{23}} = 1.3804 \times 10^{-23} \) J \( \text{K}^{-1} \):

\( E = \dfrac{3}{2} k_{B} T = 1.5 \times 1.3804 \times 10^{-23} \times 400 = 8.282 \times 10^{-21} \text{ J} \)

**Answers: (i) \( 4.986 \times 10^{6} \) J per kmol, (ii) \( 1.558 \times 10^{5} \) J per kg, (iii) \( 8.282 \times 10^{-21} \) J per molecule.**

By the Stefan-Boltzmann law, the energy radiated by a blackbody of surface area \( A \) at absolute temperature \( T \) in a time \( t \) is

\( Q = \sigma A t T^{4} \)

Convert every quantity to SI units first:

area \( A = 100 \text{ cm}^{2} = 100 \times 10^{-4} = 1 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}^{2} \) (note \( 1 \text{ cm}^{2} = 10^{-4} \text{ m}^{2} \), not \( 10^{-2} \))

temperature \( T = 227\ ^\circ \text{C} = 227 + 273 = 500 \text{ K} \)

time \( t = 1 \text{ minute} = 60 \text{ s} \)

\( \sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8} \text{ J m}^{-2} \text{s}^{-1} \text{K}^{-4} \)

\( Q = \left( 5.67 \times 10^{-8} \right) \times \left( 1 \times 10^{-2} \right) \times 60 \times (500)^{4} \)

\( (500)^{4} = 6.25 \times 10^{10} \)

\( Q = 5.67 \times 10^{-8} \times 10^{-2} \times 60 \times 6.25 \times 10^{10} \)

\( = 5.67 \times 6.25 \times 60 \times 10^{0} = 2126.25 \text{ J} \)

**Energy radiated in one minute \( = 2126.25 \text{ J} \).**

Because the body is a blackbody, \( e = 1 \) and no emissivity factor appears. The question asks for an ENERGY, not a power, which is why the 60 s is included.

A small hole in a furnace behaves as a perfect blackbody, so by the Stefan-Boltzmann law the rate at which it emits energy is

\( \dfrac{dQ}{dt} = \sigma A T^{4} \quad \Rightarrow \quad A = \dfrac{1}{\sigma T^{4}} \dfrac{dQ}{dt} \)

Convert the temperature to kelvin:

\( T = 727\ ^\circ \text{C} = 727 + 273 = 1000 \text{ K} \)

Given \( \dfrac{dQ}{dt} = 20 \text{ W} = 20 \text{ J s}^{-1} \) and \( \sigma = 5.7 \times 10^{-8} \text{ J s}^{-1} \text{m}^{-2} \text{K}^{-4} \).

\( T^{4} = (1000)^{4} = 1 \times 10^{12} \text{ K}^{4} \)

\( A = \dfrac{20}{\left( 5.7 \times 10^{-8} \right) \times \left( 1 \times 10^{12} \right)} = \dfrac{20}{5.7 \times 10^{4}} \)

\( = 3.509 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^{2} \)

**Area of the hole \( = 3.509 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^{2} \)** (about \( 3.5 \text{ cm}^{2} \)).

Note this question supplies \( \sigma = 5.7 \times 10^{-8} \) rather than the usual \( 5.67 \times 10^{-8} \); the value the stem gives is the one that must be used.

The emissive power \( R \) is the heat radiated per unit area per unit time. Hence the total heat radiated by an area \( A \) in a time \( t \) is

\( Q = R \times A \times t \)

Given \( R = 0.5 \) kcal \( \text{s}^{-1} \text{m}^{-2} \), \( A = 0.02 \text{ m}^{2} \), \( t = 20 \text{ s} \). The units of \( R \) already match those of \( A \) and \( t \), so no conversion is needed.

\( Q = 0.5 \times 0.02 \times 20 \)

\( = 0.2 \text{ kcal} \)

**Heat radiated in 20 s \( = 0.2 \text{ kcal} \)** ( \( = 200 \) cal, or about 837 J).

No temperature and no value of \( \sigma \) are needed here, because the emissive power — which is what \( \sigma T^{4} \) would have been used to find — is given directly.

Convert all three temperatures to kelvin:

\( T_{1} = 727\ ^\circ \text{C} = 1000 \text{ K} \), \( \quad T_{2} = 227\ ^\circ \text{C} = 500 \text{ K} \), \( \quad T_{0} = 27\ ^\circ \text{C} = 300 \text{ K} \)

The question asks two different things, and they have different answers.

**(a) Ratio of the rates of EMISSION.** What a body emits depends only on its own temperature: \( \dfrac{dQ}{dt} = \sigma A T^{4} \) for a blackbody. The enclosure plays no part in this.

\( \dfrac{E_{1}}{E_{2}} = \dfrac{T_{1}^{4}}{T_{2}^{4}} = \left( \dfrac{1000}{500} \right)^{4} = 2^{4} = 16 \)

\( \therefore E_{1} : E_{2} = 16 : 1 \)

**(b) Ratio of the rates of LOSS of heat.** The rate of loss is the NET rate — what the body emits minus what it absorbs from the enclosure at \( T_{0} \):

\( \dfrac{dQ}{dt} = \sigma A \left( T^{4} - T_{0}^{4} \right) \)

\( \dfrac{R_{1}}{R_{2}} = \dfrac{T_{1}^{4} - T_{0}^{4}}{T_{2}^{4} - T_{0}^{4}} = \dfrac{(1000)^{4} - (300)^{4}}{(500)^{4} - (300)^{4}} \)

\( = \dfrac{1.0000 \times 10^{12} - 0.0081 \times 10^{12}}{0.0625 \times 10^{12} - 0.0081 \times 10^{12}} = \dfrac{0.9919 \times 10^{12}}{0.0544 \times 10^{12}} \)

\( = 18.23 \)

\( \therefore R_{1} : R_{2} = 18.23 : 1 \)

**Rates of emission \( 16 : 1 \); rates of loss of heat \( 18.23 : 1 \).**

The loss ratio is the LARGER of the two, because subtracting the same absorbed term \( \sigma A T_{0}^{4} \) from both takes proportionately much more away from the cooler body than from the hotter one.

**Shape of the curve.** Plotting the radiant power per unit area per unit wavelength range \( R_{\lambda} \) against \( \lambda \) for a blackbody at 280 K gives a single continuous, single-peaked curve: it starts at zero at \( \lambda = 0 \), rises steeply to a maximum at \( \lambda_{\max} \), then falls and tails off asymptotically towards zero at long wavelengths. Because 280 K is a low temperature, the curve is a low, broad one whose peak lies far out in the infrared — well to the right of the visible band — and the area under it, which equals the total emission \( \sigma T^{4} \), is small. A curve for any higher temperature would lie entirely above it with its peak further to the left, and the two would never cross.

**Position of the peak.** By Wien's displacement law,

\( \lambda_{\max} = \dfrac{b}{T} \)

with \( b = 2.897 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m K} \) and \( T = 280 \text{ K} \) (already absolute, so no conversion is needed):

\( \lambda_{\max} = \dfrac{2.897 \times 10^{-3}}{280} = 1.035 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m} \)

**\( \lambda_{\max} = 1.035 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m} = 10.35\ \mu\text{m} = 103500\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}} \).**

**Region of the spectrum.** The visible band runs from about \( 4 \times 10^{-7} \) m to \( 7 \times 10^{-7} \) m. At \( 1.035 \times 10^{-5} \) m this wavelength is roughly fifteen times longer than the red end of the visible spectrum, so it lies in the **INFRARED region**.

This is why the Earth, warmed by visible sunlight, re-radiates in the infrared, and why a thermal-imaging camera must be built to detect infrared rather than visible light.

The sphere is hotter than its surroundings, so it loses heat by radiation at the NET rate

\( \dfrac{dQ}{dt} = \sigma A \left( T^{4} - T_{0}^{4} \right) \)

(the sphere is blackened and to be treated as a blackbody, so \( e = 1 \)). To hold its temperature steady, energy must be supplied at exactly this rate.

Surface area of the sphere, with \( r = 2.5 \text{ cm} = 2.5 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m} \) and \( \pi = 3.1416 \):

\( A = 4 \pi r^{2} = 4 \times 3.1416 \times \left( 2.5 \times 10^{-2} \right)^{2} = 7.854 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}^{2} \)

Temperatures in kelvin:

\( T = 110\ ^\circ \text{C} = 383 \text{ K} \) (the sphere), \( \quad T_{0} = 100\ ^\circ \text{C} = 373 \text{ K} \) (the chamber)

\( T^{4} = (383)^{4} = 2.1518 \times 10^{10} \text{ K}^{4} \), \( \quad T_{0}^{4} = (373)^{4} = 1.9357 \times 10^{10} \text{ K}^{4} \)

\( T^{4} - T_{0}^{4} = 2.161 \times 10^{9} \text{ K}^{4} \)

\( \dfrac{dQ}{dt} = \left( 5.670 \times 10^{-8} \right) \times \left( 7.854 \times 10^{-3} \right) \times \left( 2.161 \times 10^{9} \right) \)

\( = 4.4532 \times 10^{-10} \times 2.161 \times 10^{9} = 0.9623 \text{ W} \)

**Energy must be supplied at about \( 0.962 \text{ W} \)** (0.9622 W using unrounded fourth powers, 0.9624 W as printed if \( T^{4} \) and \( T_{0}^{4} \) are each rounded to five significant figures first — the difference is rounding of the intermediate step, not of the method).

The temperature DIFFERENCE is only 10 K, but it is the difference of the fourth powers that matters, not the difference of the temperatures; \( \left( 383 - 373 \right)^{4} \) would be a completely different and meaningless quantity.

By Wien's displacement law the peak of a blackbody's spectrum satisfies \( \lambda_{\max} T = b \), so

\( T = \dfrac{b}{\lambda_{\max}} \), with \( b = 2.897 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m K} \)

Every wavelength must first be expressed in METRES, since \( b \) is in m K.

**(a) \( \lambda_{\max} = 700 \text{ nm} = 700 \times 10^{-9} = 7 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m} \)** (visible)

\( T = \dfrac{2.897 \times 10^{-3}}{7 \times 10^{-7}} = 4.139 \times 10^{3} = 4138 \text{ K} \)

**(b) \( \lambda_{\max} = 3 \text{ cm} = 3 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m} \)** (microwave)

\( T = \dfrac{2.897 \times 10^{-3}}{3 \times 10^{-2}} = 9.657 \times 10^{-2} = 0.09657 \text{ K} \)

**(c) \( \lambda_{\max} = 3 \text{ m} \)** (short radio waves)

\( T = \dfrac{2.897 \times 10^{-3}}{3} = 9.657 \times 10^{-4} = 0.9657 \times 10^{-3} \text{ K} \)

**Answers: (a) 4138 K, (b) 0.09657 K, (c) \( 0.9657 \times 10^{-3} \) K.**

The temperatures fall as the peak wavelength rises, which is the inverse proportionality of Wien's law: a body that peaks in the visible must be thousands of kelvin, whereas one peaking in the microwave or radio region is a small fraction of a kelvin above absolute zero. Cases (b) and (c) are far colder than anything on Earth; the cosmic microwave background, at 2.7 K, peaks near 1 mm.
